question: A communications officer receives a first draft that is accurate but far too shallow for the intended briefing. Which two follow-up actions are most likely to improve the second attempt? Select two.
options: A) Send the identical prompt again in the hope that the next attempt comes out stronger.
B) Show a passage from last quarter's briefing as an example of the depth wanted.
C) Append the words "be thorough and detailed" to the end of the original request text.
D) Supply the figures and case details the briefing must cover, which were not in the prompt.
E) Reply that the draft was disappointing and ask Claude to try considerably harder now.
correct_answers: B) Show a passage from last quarter's briefing as an example of the depth wanted.
D) Supply the figures and case details the briefing must cover, which were not in the prompt.
explanations: Resending an unchanged prompt is the least productive iteration. The specification is identical, so any improvement is chance rather than something that can be relied on.
Correct. An example communicates a standard that adjectives cannot, and it works even where the officer would struggle to describe the wanted depth in words.
Generic intensifiers are among the weakest edits available. "Thorough" is undefined, so it gives Claude no target it can aim the second draft at.
Correct. Shallowness is usually an information problem. Claude cannot write to a depth the prompt never supplied the material for, so adding the substance is the direct fix.
Negative feedback without specifics tells Claude that something was wrong but not what, so the next draft varies at random rather than converging.
